title: Make Work Pay: ending one-sided flexibility, reforms of zero hours and similar contracts
date_evidence: meta-govuk:first-published-at: 2026-06-02T09:30:02+01:00 ; visible: Published: 2 June 2026 / Last updated: 12 August 2026
key_claim: The consultation on how the Employment Rights Act 2025 guaranteed-hours duty will be implemented ran from 2 June 2026 to 25 August 2026 and is now closed, with the operative parameters left to regulations.
frame_summary: This source is arguing that the substance of the zero-hours reform is a set of design choices still open at consultation, not a settled prohibition, and that the parameters decide the policy.
verbatim_quote: This consultation ran from 9:30am on 2 June 2026 to 11:59pm on 25 August 2026
notes: Landing page for the consultation and its documents. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page during the 19/09/2026 verification pass; audit_verbatim_quote_provenance.py returned NETWORK_ERROR because the build sandbox has no egress to this domain.

publisher: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
title: Right to guaranteed hours: options assessment
date_evidence: IA number: DBT-017-26-CMRR / RPC reference number: RPC-DBT-26155-OA(1) / Date: 12/08/2026
key_claim: The government's own options assessment tells employers to update contracts, payroll and rostering systems to track hours and generate guaranteed-hours offers, and to implement workforce planning and demand forecasting tools.
frame_summary: This source is arguing that compliance with the duty is a systems and forecasting problem for employers rather than a one-off contractual change.
verbatim_quote: Update employment contracts, payroll, and rostering systems to embed compliance processes associated with tracking hours and making guaranteed hours offers.
verbatim_list: Implement workforce planning and demand forecasting tools to align staffing levels with guaranteed hours and reduce reliance on ad hoc scheduling.
notes: PDF on the government assets domain. Quotes confirmed by hand during the 19/09/2026 verification pass; the provenance audit carries a systemic override for PDF byte streams and the sandbox has no egress to this domain.

title: RPC opinion: right to guaranteed hours
key_claim: The independent scrutiny body found the quantified costs capture only administration and planning burdens and leave the economic cost of reduced scheduling and workforce flexibility largely unassessed, rating the scorecard weak.
frame_summary: This source is arguing that the government has not measured the cost that matters, namely the loss of scheduling flexibility, so the published cost range understates what the duty does to operations.
verbatim_quote: The quantified costs capture only administration and planning burdens, while leaving the substantive economic cost of reduced scheduling and workforce flexibility largely unassessed.
verbatim_list: However, the OA also notes that some costs, including system, tracking and workforce-planning costs, overlap with the related zero-hours reforms and may be subject to double counting.
notes: Quote confirmed by hand during the 19/09/2026 verification pass; sandbox has no egress to gov.uk. The weak rating triggers mandatory resubmission at final impact-assessment stage.

title: The zero hours provisions of the Employment Rights Act: diversionary tactics (Zoe Adams)
key_claim: The Act preserves the lawful status of zero-hours arrangements and supplies limited protections that fall well short of a right to a fair schedule or to sufficient work.
frame_summary: This source is arguing that the zero-hours provisions are a diversion from stronger alternatives, because they regulate the offer of hours while leaving the underlying contractual form intact.
verbatim_quote: This dilemma presents itself particularly acutely in the context of the new Zero Hour provisions of the Employment Rights Act 2025.
notes: Peer-reviewed, structural anchor in the 3-6 month band, cited inline like any other source. Abstract and introduction are open; the substantive analysis sits behind a paywall, so the scan relies only on the open text.

publisher: The Work Foundation at Lancaster University
title: Record 1.24 million people on zero-hours contracts as workers report work-life chaos
date_evidence: 10 August 2026 11:00 (visible byline block directly under the headline)
key_claim: Work Foundation analysis of ONS data puts a record 1.24 million people on zero-hours contracts, with 32.8% depending on the contract for full-time work and 77% not in full-time education.
frame_summary: This source is arguing that zero-hours flexibility runs one way in the employer's favour and that the regulations must set demanding notice, cancellation and threshold parameters to change that.
verbatim_quote: A record 1.24 million people are now employed on zero-hours contracts, as new research reveals how unpredictable shifts, last-minute cancellations and fluctuating pay can create "work-life chaos" for workers.
verbatim_list: Analysis by the Work Foundation of ONS data indicates that a record number of workers depend on their zero-hour contract for full-time work (32.8%) and are not in full-time education (77%).
notes: The page's CMS meta tags are a template artefact showing 2020 dates; the visible byline of 10 August 2026 is the publication date, corroborated by ITV News coverage timestamped 2026-08-10. The qualitative core is a nine-worker diary study, so only the ONS-derived figures are used here.

title: Overall cost of zero hours proposals to business starts at £300m
date_evidence: meta-article:published_time: 2026-08-13T09:50:09+00:00 ; visible: by Adam McCulloch 13 Aug 2026
key_claim: Reporting the government's own analysis: the share of employee jobs at or below the threshold runs from 11% (3.3 million) at 8 hours per week to 99% (28.6 million) at 48 hours, and the net cost to business is £300 million to £1.4 billion a year.
frame_summary: This source is arguing that the threshold, not the principle, decides the scale of the reform, and that the government has conceded a wide and uncertain cost range.
verbatim_quote: The document said the share of employee jobs potentially at or below the threshold rose from 11% (3.3 million employee jobs) at 8 hours per week to 20% (5.9 million) at 20 hours, 34% (9.7 million) at 32 hours, 91% (26.2 million) at 40 hours and 99% (28.6 million) at 48 hours.
verbatim_list: Ministers have conceded that its proposed zero hours reforms as a whole could lead to a net cost of between £300 million and £1.4 billion per year for UK businesses.
notes: Trade press restating figures from the government's published analysis. Quotes confirmed by hand during the 19/09/2026 verification pass.

title: CIPD zero-hours response outlines cost concerns
date_evidence: by Jo Faragher 25 Aug 2026 (meta-article:published_time 2026-08-24T23:12:16+00:00, which is 00:12 BST on 25 August)
key_claim: The CIPD's consultation response argues employers will substitute temporary, casual and self-employed labour rather than convert zero-hours work into guaranteed hours, with a third of employers already expecting to increase contractor use.
frame_summary: This source is arguing that the duty will displace insecure work into other supply channels rather than reduce it, which is the strongest sourced case against the reform achieving its stated aim.
verbatim_quote: Employers are unlikely to replace zero hours contracts with more permanent, guaranteed hours jobs, and will instead increase their use of temporary workers, short-term casual staff, and freelancers.
verbatim_list: Previous CIPD research has found that a third of employers that use zero-hours arrangements expect to increase their use of self-employed contractors and other temporary or casual staff as a result of the reforms.
notes: Counter-evidence. Trade press reporting a professional body's consultation response; the underlying position is the CIPD's, so it is positional as well as secondary.

title: Zero hours consultation: our response
key_claim: The trade body argues the reference period for guaranteed hours should be 26 weeks rather than the government's preferred 12, to reflect seasonal work patterns.
frame_summary: This source is arguing that the reference period is the parameter that determines whether the duty reflects a genuine working pattern or a seasonal artefact.
verbatim_quote: In particular, the reference period for guaranteed hours should be set much higher than the Government's preference of 12 weeks.
verbatim_list: There is a danger that over-regulating flexible work actually increases work instability, rather than decrease it, which would undermine the Government's agenda to get people back into work.
notes: Industry association, so Tier 3 and inherently positional. Used for the reference-period parameter, which no Tier 1 in-window source states in fetchable form.
